summary:
Wisconsin is a state of the United States and stands under the national framework carried by the national record; the findings below are the Wisconsin-specific layer. A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Wisconsin in its low-risk group, alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia and the District of Columbia, describing jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults while not taking extraordinary steps to protect them.

No statewide law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity, and gender identity is not a protected class under the state hate-crime statute, though sexual orientation is. Prosecutors have sometimes used perceived sexual orientation as the route to charge crimes motivated by a victim's gender identity. Local protection is patchwork: as of 29 May 2025, 21 per cent of the state's population lived in the ten cities with full employment, housing and public-accommodation ordinances covering gender identity, and 12 per cent in cities with partial ordinances. Dane and Milwaukee counties and the cities of Appleton, Cudahy, De Pere, Janesville, Madison, Milwaukee and Racine ban gender-identity discrimination; Oshkosh and Stevens Point extend protection only to transgender city employees. Executive Order #1, issued 7 January 2019, prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression in state employment, state contracting and the provision of state services, and directs state agencies to adopt and enforce nondiscrimination policies.

Wisconsin has no law barring transgender people from using government-building bathrooms or facilities consistent with their gender identity, no law defining sex to exclude transgender people, and no restriction on drag performance. The state's equality-map profile, current to 29 May 2025, records no ban on best-practice medical care for transgender youth and no shield law protecting providers or patients from out-of-state action.

Identity documents are the main friction point. Gender-marker change on a Wisconsin driver's licence is permitted only in limited circumstances, and change on a birth certificate is restricted: a person born in the state who has completed sex reassignment surgery may amend the birth certificate on documentation of the surgery and a name change. Neither licence nor birth certificate offers an X gender-neutral option, and the name-change process is restrictive.

State law does not ban gender-affirming care for minors. Governor Tony Evers vetoed Assembly Bill 465 on 6 December 2023, blocking a legislature-passed ban on gender-affirming health care for people under 18; he had earlier vetoed a June 2023 budget provision that would have barred Medicaid coverage of sexual reassignment surgery and other gender-affirming care for all individuals regardless of age. Care access nonetheless contracted under federal funding pressure: UW Health and Children's Wisconsin each announced on 13 January 2026 that they would pause gender-affirming pharmacologic care for patients under 18 after the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services said it would deny Medicaid and Medicare payments to hospitals providing such care to minors. Mental and behavioural health services continued. Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul joined a multistate coalition seeking to block the HHS declaration. The pause follows federal funding pressure on Wisconsin hospitals rather than any state ban.

Marriage between two people regardless of sex has been recognised since 6 October 2014, when the Supreme Court declined the appeal in Wolf v. Walker and the district court's stay was lifted. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can expect that marriage to be recognised. Parenting rules allow individuals to adopt without regard to sexual orientation and married couples to adopt; access to IVF and artificial insemination is permitted, with state recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother only if she is married. A September 2016 federal ruling required both parents to be recorded on birth certificates, and since 1 July 2021 birth certificates offer gender-neutral 'spouse' and 'parent 1'/'parent 2' options.

Private, non-commercial sexual conduct between consenting adults has been legal since 1983, when the state's sodomy provisions were repealed; the repealing legislation stated that Wisconsin did not approve of sexual conduct outside marriage.

The Milwaukee Police Department stopped listing the gender of crime victims in September 2023, alongside race, in order to avoid misgendering transgender people.
tangentialFactors:
Bills restricting gender-affirming care and transgender sports participation have been introduced repeatedly. A 2021 bill barring transgender women from teams aligning with their gender passed the Assembly on party lines but was never voted on in the Senate; it was re-introduced in 2023, and a bill passed by the legislature in 2024 was vetoed by the governor on 2 April 2024. The bill's sponsor called the veto 'disgusting'. Evers had promised the veto since the bill was introduced, and Democrats did not have enough votes to stop its passage in the legislature. On medical care, a 2021 bill prohibiting insurers from covering gender-affirming care procedures for minors failed in committee; a re-introduced bill passed the Assembly on 12 October 2023 and the Senate on 17 October 2023 and was vetoed on 6 December 2023.

Public hearings in October 2023 on bills to ban gender-affirming care for transgender youth, including the 'Help Not Harm Act' based on model legislation, and to restrict transgender sports participation were marked by misinformation, with lawmaker questions indicating gaps in basic knowledge. The WIAA and NCAA retained their own policies addressing transgender athletes.

A 2017 PRRI poll found 73 per cent supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity, with 20 per cent opposed; 66 per cent supported marriage between same-sex couples, with 26 per cent opposed and 8 per cent unsure.

In October 2023 Evers, speaking to 'LGBTQ folks, especially our trans kids', said he would veto any bill that makes Wisconsin a less welcoming, less inclusive and less safe place to be who you are. Introductions of the transgender athlete and medical-care bills sparked significant backlash from organisational and community advocates, including Fair Wisconsin, GSAFE and the ACLU of Wisconsin.
localsOnly:
People in prison are entitled to hormone therapy. The 2005 Inmate Sex Change Prevention Act, which denied hormone therapy to prisoners undergoing sex reassignment, was ruled unconstitutional unanimously by the Seventh Circuit on 5 August 2011, and the Supreme Court denied the state's appeal on 26 March 2012.

Sex reassignment surgery was explicitly included in Wisconsin Medicaid for state employees from January 2019 and was ordered extended to non-government employees in May 2019 under the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment. A June 2023 budget bill passed by both houses banning Medicaid coverage of sexual reassignment surgery and other gender-affirming healthcare for all individuals regardless of age was vetoed under line-item veto power. Private insurance and Medicaid were barred from excluding transgender-specific care.

Persons on Wisconsin's sex offender registry are not allowed to change their names, with no exception for transgender people.

Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been banned statewide in employment, housing, education, credit and all public accommodations since 1982, making Wisconsin the first U.S. state to do so; sexual orientation is a protected class in the hate-crime law and under a 2001 law prohibiting sexual-orientation discrimination in schools.

Conversion therapy on minors is banned in 14 communities, including Milwaukee (March 2018), Madison (July 2018), Eau Claire (October 2018), Cudahy, Shorewood, Racine, Glendale, Sheboygan, Superior, West Allis (September 2020), Kenosha (October 2020), Sun Prairie, Appleton and La Crosse. Kenosha's ordinance carries a maximum fine of 1,000 dollars plus costs, up to 90 days in the Kenosha County Jail and possible suspension of driving privileges for up to five years. A June 2021 executive order barred state taxpayer funds from supporting conversion therapy on LGBT minors. Statewide ban efforts were blocked in June 2020 and January 2023, and in July 2025 the Wisconsin Supreme Court ruled 4-3 that such bans can be enacted by regulation and executive order.
outOfScopeNotes: The July 2026 assessment's criteria and methodology are not published in the source; the low-risk grouping is a comparative label, not a statement of legal protection. The equality-map profile is current to 29 May 2025 and does not capture later legislative changes. Whether the January 2026 pause on pharmacologic care for under-18s at UW Health and Children's Wisconsin remains in force is not sourced. The specific documentation standard for the limited driver's licence gender-marker change is not stated in the inventory. The number of municipalities with conversion-therapy bans is given as 14, but the source names 13. Whether prosecutors' use of perceived sexual orientation to charge gender-identity-motivated crimes is systematic is not documented with case counts. The status of the multistate challenge to the HHS declaration is unresolved.
